items.canonical_answer: Urbanisation is the growth in the proportion of a country's population living in urban areas. It is a rising share of the whole population, which is not the same as one city growing: a capital can grow while the share stands still, if the countryside grows too.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning of the term, the rising proportion of the population living in urban areas; the proportion is what separates it from the growth of a single city.

objective_titles: Identify and suggest reasons for rapid urban growth

items.prompt: Explain why the populations of cities in developing countries grow so quickly.
items.canonical_answer: Because two engines run at once. Rural-urban migration adds arrivals, pushed by failing farm incomes, drought years and schooling that ends early, and pulled by specific gains, jobs in factories and offices, secondary school places, hospital care and piped water. Natural increase then adds births, because the arrivals are mostly young adults, so the city holds many births and few elderly deaths, which means the population keeps climbing even in a year when few newcomers arrive.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3, each a because-and-so step: migration, with a named push or pull; natural increase, because the young population structure holds many births; so both engines together, which causes the speed of the growth.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.7 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Identify and suggest reasons for rapid urban growth

items.prompt:
The table shows the share of four countries' populations living in urban areas:

| country | share in urban areas, 2000 | share in urban areas, 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| A, low income | 22 per cent | 48 per cent |
| B, low income | 31 per cent | 56 per cent |
| C, middle income | 58 per cent | 71 per cent |
| D, high income | 79 per cent | 82 per cent |

Describe the trends shown.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows the share living in urban areas rising in all four countries, so urbanisation is happening everywhere but at very different speeds. The two low-income countries climbed 26 and 25 percentage points between 2000 and 2025, 22 to 48 per cent and 31 to 56 per cent, whereas the high-income country added 3 points, from 79 to 82 per cent. The trend shown is that urbanisation runs fastest where the urban share started lowest, which means the developing countries are urbanising most quickly and the already-urban rich country is close to the end of the process.
marking_guidance: Reading: the trend read from the table, shares rising in all four countries, fastest in the low-income pair (1 mark).

Values: the figures quoted, 22 to 48 per cent and 79 to 82 per cent (1 mark); so the answer draws the meaning, the rising share is what urbanisation measures and it rises fastest late-comer countries (1 mark).

objective_titles: Identify and suggest reasons for rapid urban growth

items.prompt:
At a bus station in a fast-growing city, a survey of 200 new arrivals gave these reasons for coming:

| reason named | arrivals naming it |
|---|---|
| work in factories, offices or markets | 138 |
| secondary school and college places | 96 |
| clinic and hospital care | 74 |
| the farm at home had failed three years running | 61 |

Suggest what the survey shows about why the city is growing so fast.
items.canonical_answer: The survey suggests the city grows because specific, pictureable pulls outweigh the farm: 138 of the 200 arrivals name work in factories, offices or markets, and 96 name secondary school and college places, which a reader can picture exactly. The pushes matter as well, because 61 arrivals name a farm that failed three years running. So the table shows both engines of the move together, and it suggests the decision to arrive follows a picture of jobs and schools, not a vague idea of a better life.
marking_guidance: Resource: the evidence used, 138 of 200 for work and 96 for school places (1 mark).

Reasons: the pulls are named specifically, so the answer says exactly what draws people (1 mark); therefore the push matters too, because 61 arrivals name the failed farm, so both ends of the move appear (1 mark).

objective_titles: Identify and suggest reasons for rapid urban growth

items.prompt: Explaining why families move from a rural area to a city, a learner writes: 'They move because the city has a better standard of living, more facilities and is more developed.' Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is that the reasons are vague: a reader cannot picture exactly what is better, so the answer does not yet name a pull. The reasoned answer names the specific pulls instead: more jobs in factories and offices, secondary school places, hospital care and piped water. The test is whether a reader could picture exactly what is better, and facilities could be anything, whereas a secondary school with places to spare cannot.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named, vague terms explain nothing, so no pull is actually given.
1 mark: the correct idea, the specific pulls named instead, jobs, schools, hospital care, piped water, so the reader can picture what is better.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.7 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Identify and suggest reasons for rapid urban growth

items.prompt: Asked to define a rural area, a learner writes: 'A rural area is somewhere behind in development, with no facilities and poor services.' Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is defining a rural area by its lack of development, which is not the same as what the term means: a rural area is countryside, with farmland and small settlements, and a village with a school and a clinic is still rural. The test is whether the definition describes the land and settlement, and the learner's answer describes wealth and services instead, so it does not define the term.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named, the answer confuses being less developed with being rural, which is not the same thing.
1 mark: the correct idea, a rural area is countryside with farmland and small settlements, so the definition describes the land and its settlement.

items.prompt: A newspaper column calls the young adults who leave Namibia's villages for its cities "the generation that abandoned the land". Suggest how far this judgement is fair.
items.canonical_answer: The judgement is partly unfair. Abandoned fits the effect of the move: villages lose their young adults, so the population structure ages and farm labour grows scarce, which the column sees plainly. But the move is not a desertion, because migrants send money home, and those remittances pay school fees and put seed back into the farms, and the movers leave for pictureable gains, jobs, schools and hospital care, rather than out of carelessness. The fairer judgement is that the generation moved: the villages lost labour and gained support at the same time, so the column's word is one half of the truth.
marking_guidance: Judgement: 1 mark for a stated decision, partly unfair, with the sense of how far.
Because: 1 mark for the reasoning weighed, lost labour and ageing against remittances and the pictured gains.
Evidence: 1 mark for the examples used, remittances paying school fees and the named pulls, so the judgement rests on evidence.

objective_titles: Identify and suggest reasons for rapid urban growth

items.prompt: The photograph shows the newest part of a fast-growing city: hundreds of self-built houses of sheet metal and concrete block, paths that flood after rain because there are no drains, one standpipe with a queue of containers, and power lines on poles above the rooftops. Suggest how urban growth has changed this part of the city, and one change that would reduce the worst of it.
items.canonical_answer: Urban growth has turned this fringe from open land into a crowded settlement faster than services could follow: the photograph shows houses without drains, so rain floods the paths, and a single standpipe with a queue, which suggests the water supply serves a fraction of the people now living there. The change that would reduce the worst of it is upgrading the settlement in place, adding drains, taps and power to the homes people have already built, because upgrading reaches more households for the same budget than clearing and rebuilding would.
marking_guidance: Resource: the evidence used, the flooding paths and the single standpipe with its queue (1 mark).

Reasons: growth outpaced the services, so housing arrived before drains and water (1 mark); therefore upgrading in place is the suggested change, because it reduces the flooding and queueing the photograph shows (1 mark).

items.prompt: A city has one budget for housing. One proposal is to spend it upgrading the informal settlements; another is to spend it on rural roads and clinics so that fewer people leave the countryside. Suggest which the city should choose, with reasons.
items.canonical_answer: The better decision is upgrading the informal settlements, because the people are already there: the city's growth has outpaced its services, and drains, taps and toilets added to existing homes relieve the flooding, queues and disease that growth has already caused, at a cost per household far below clearing and rebuilding. The rural proposal aims at the cause rather than the consequence, which is worth doing, but rural roads and clinics take years to slow the migration, while the settlements need water now. The judgement is therefore upgrading first, with the rural programme started beside it when funds allow.
marking_guidance: Judgement: 1 mark for a stated decision, upgrading first.
Because: 1 mark for the reasoning weighed, the consequence is present now while the cause takes years to act on.
Evidence: 1 mark for the examples and costs used, drains and taps per household against years of rural building, so the judgement rests on evidence.

objective_titles: Describe the impacts of urban growth on both rural and urban areas, along with possible solutions to reduce the negative impacts

items.prompt:
The table compares a rural district with the city settlement its young adults have moved to:

| | rural home district | city settlement |
|---|---|---|
| people aged 15 to 30 | 14 per cent | 39 per cent |
| average age | 42 | 24 |
| households with piped water | 58 per cent | 71 per cent |
| dwellings built in the last ten years | 3 per cent | 31 per cent |

Describe the impacts of urban growth the table shows on each area.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows the move in both areas' figures. The city settlement is young, 39 per cent aged 15 to 30 against the district's 14 per cent, with an average age of 24 against 42, and it is building fast, 31 per cent of dwellings under ten years old, which means arrivals are adding homes quicker than services follow. The rural district shows the other end of the process: its 15-to-30 share has thinned to 14 per cent and its average age has reached 42, so the values show an ageing home district supplying young adults to a young city. Its piped-water share, 58 per cent against the city's 71 per cent, shows the countryside is the worse served of the two.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table, a young city against an ageing countryside (1 mark).

Values: the figures quoted, 39 against 14 per cent, average ages 24 and 42, dwellings 31 against 3 per cent (1 mark); so the answer links both to migration, which means the table describes one process seen from its two ends (1 mark).

items.prompt: Asked to describe the impacts of urban growth on the rural areas people leave, a learner writes: 'Squatter settlements grow, traffic gets worse and water becomes short.' Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is answering about the city when the question names the rural areas people leave: squatter settlements, traffic and city water are urban impacts. The impacts the question asks for are rural ones, fewer young adults, so the population structure ages and farm labour grows scarce, and the money migrants send home. The test is which area the question names, and here it names the countryside, so every point should be about it.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named, urban impacts given where the question asks for rural ones, which is answering about the wrong area.
1 mark: the correct idea, rural impacts instead, the ageing population structure, scarcer farm labour and remittances, so the answer matches the area the question names.

items.prompt: For Lagos in Nigeria, describe two features that show how fast it has grown.
items.canonical_answer: Lagos is one of the largest cities in Africa, with an estimated 16.5 million people in 2024 and growth of hundreds of thousands a year, so its population has multiplied within living memory. It was Nigeria's capital until 1991 and remains its chief port and commercial city, so new arrivals keep coming from the rural north and east of Nigeria and from neighbouring countries.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all: the size and growth figure with its year; the port and capital role that keeps drawing migrants.
Each feature is a fact of the named city, Lagos, not a general point about growth.

items.prompt: For Lagos in Nigeria, explain why migrants keep arriving from the rural areas.
items.canonical_answer: Because Lagos concentrates what the countryside lacks, this example shows the pull at work: the port at Apapa and the factories and markets around it offer wages a small farm cannot match, and the office towers of Victoria Island add office work beside them. Secondary schools and universities sit there too, so families follow work with schooling, and the hospital care the city gathers pulls the sick and the old as well. The pushes matter as well, because failing farm incomes and insecurity in the north-east send young adults down the roads to the coast, which means the arrivals come for pictureable gains, jobs, schools and care, and they keep coming while those gains stay concentrated in the city.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 4, each from the named example: the port, factories and markets give work; the offices and schools add further pulls; so the pushes, failing farm incomes and insecurity, send the migrants; therefore the gains stay concentrated in Lagos, which explains why the arrivals continue.

items.prompt: For a named rapidly growing urban area in a developing country, describe its growth and the impacts of that growth on the city and on the rural areas its migrants leave. [7]
items.canonical_answer: Lagos, in Nigeria, is one of the largest cities in Africa, with an estimated 16.5 million people in 2024 and growth of hundreds of thousands a year, drawn by the port at Apapa, the factories and markets around it and the offices of Victoria Island; it was Nigeria's capital until 1991 and remains its chief port and commercial city. In the city, the growth shows at Makoko, the settlement of houses on stilts above the lagoon, where thousands of families live without secure land or piped water, and in the daily traffic, which the Bus Rapid Transit system, launched in 2008, now carries in dedicated lanes; Eko Atlantic, a district reclaimed from the sea behind a long sea wall, adds the office and apartment ground the old city lacks. The rural areas the migrants leave grow older, because their young adults have gone, and lean on the money sent home. Both ends show one process: a city of pictureable gains, wages, schools and hospitals, pulling young people from a countryside that then ages, so the solutions that work serve the people already there and develop the villages at the same time.
marking_guidance: Level 1 (1-3): simple statements about cities growing, with no named example or only general points.
Level 2 (4-6): developed and linked statements about a named urban area, capped at 5 if no named example is given.
Level 3 (7): comprehensive statements with place-specific detail, Lagos, Apapa, Makoko, the 2008 transit system, Eko Atlantic, covering the growth, the urban impacts and the rural impacts.

items.prompt:
The table shows one country's population over 35 years:

| year | total population | people living in urban areas | share in urban areas |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1990 | 1 000 000 | 280 000 | 28 per cent |
| 2005 | 1 400 000 | 490 000 | 35 per cent |
| 2025 | 2 000 000 | 1 000 000 | 50 per cent |

(a) Identify the year in which half the population lived in urban areas. [1]
(b) Describe two changes shown between 1990 and 2025. [2]
(c) Suggest reasons for the rise in the share living in urban areas. [3]
(d) Suggest one way the government could reduce the pressure this growth puts on the city. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) 2025.
(b) The share living in urban areas rose from 28 per cent to 50 per cent, and the urban population more than tripled, from 280 000 to 1 000 000 people, while the total population only doubled.
(c) Rural-urban migration pulls people in with specific gains, jobs in factories and offices, secondary school places, hospital care and piped water, and pushes them out with failing farm incomes and drought years. Natural increase adds the second engine, because the arrivals are mostly young adults, so the city holds many births and few elderly deaths, and the urban share climbs faster than the count of arrivals alone.
(d) The government could upgrade the informal settlements in place, adding water points, drains and toilets to the homes already built, because that relieves the worst of the pressure at the lowest cost per household; or it could develop rural schools and clinics, so that staying becomes a real choice and the migration slows.
marking_guidance: Resource: (a) 1 mark for 2025 read from the table.
Marks and figures: (b) 2 marks, 1 per change with the values, the share from 28 to 50 per cent and the urban count from 280 000 to 1 000 000.
Evidence: (c) 3 marks, the specific pulls named (1), natural increase because of the young population structure (1), so both engines together with a because (1).
Values: (d) 2 marks, one way named with its mechanism, upgrading or rural development, with figures or examples of what it adds, so the suggestion is reasoned.
